summary: Reviewed the round-2 candidate (sha256 96b0e8e4…, identical in optimize_definition_output.json, .ledger.json and .best_kernel.py) against the supplied definition, oracle, correctness/timing workloads, evaluation contract, and prior preflight/evaluate/review artifacts. The candidate is a genuine Triton implementation of moe_sum_reduce (input.float().sum(dim=1).mul(routed_scaling_factor).to(input.dtype)): it contains no torch.ops / torch fallback, no reference import or dispatcher registration, no cached or shape-keyed constant outputs, no host synchronization and no environment mutation, so I found no P0 code or test-contract defect. Its two-path dispatch is arithmetically sound: the mask-free contiguous path is only taken when block_m (power of two ≤16) divides T and block_n (power of two ≤1024) divides H and input.is_contiguous(), so grid (T/block_m, H/block_n) and the flat offsets m*(K*H)+n+k*H are all in bounds; every other case (non-contiguous, odd H/T) falls to the masked strided kernel with real runtime strides. fp32 accumulation then one fp32 multiply then store cast to the input dtype reproduces the reference's fp32-sum/cast-back order, consistent with the reported abs_err 0, and the returned tensor is freshly allocated (matches effects.mutates=[] and returns_alias_of={}). The catalog oracle (oracle.py) does not import or call the candidate, and its bf16 tolerance (atol=rtol=1.5e-2) matches the workload tolerance (0.015, matched_ratio 1.0); the review_tests evaluate.json reference_source='primary' with all speedups ≈1.0 is a reference-as-solution sanity check, not proof of correctness. The findings below are advisory: (1) the authoritative final_verification retest measures three of five timing workloads below the reference (0.879/0.920/0.892) while the run summary claims every shape was lifted to 0.925/0.990/1.009 and the ledger keeps a different best_geo_mean; (2) no explicit correctness case exercises block_m>1, so the BM=16/BN=1024 path used by all five timing shapes has no supplied numerical validation; (3) the supplied test-review artifact is an explicit skip bound to a different subject sha and therefore does not evidence acceptance of this candidate's test contract.

findings.evidence: optimize_definition_output.json:13-93 (final_verification, compared_to='original_round') — 'after' latencies vs reference latencies give speedups 0.089935/0.102314=0.879 (00000), 0.093627/0.101806=0.920 (00001), 0.090522/0.101485=0.892 (00002), 0.252925/0.103046=2.455 (00003), 2.413445/0.482605=5.001 (00004); geo_mean 1.5466648665624774. optimize_definition_output.json:103 states the shapes were 'lift[ed] … 1/8/64 tokens from 0.716x/0.726x/0.752x to 0.925x/0.990x/1.009x', which are the round-2 in-round numbers, not the retest. .ledger.json:6 best_geo_mean=1.6234482787134883 with .ledger.json:221-222 geo_mean=1.6234482787134883 / min_speedup=0.9254903423611779, whereas optimize_definition_output.json:5 best_geo_mean=1.5466648665624774 and :7 search_best_geo_mean=1.6234482787134883.
findings.reason: The authoritative retest that produced the recorded best_geo_mean (1.5467) measures three of the five timing workloads slower than the reference (0.879x/0.920x/0.892x, min_speedup ≈0.879), i.e. only the two large shapes carry the geo_mean. The run summary and the ledger instead present the pre-retest round-2 per-shape speedups and a 1.6234 best_geo_mean. Performance PASSED with geo_mean>1 does not imply per-workload speedup>1; the ~8-19% small-shape drift is consistent with the dispatch-bound regime described in .ledger.json:447, but the reported claims do not match the verified measurement and ledger/definition disagree on the headline number.
findings.requested_change: Treat final_verification as the authoritative measurement: report min_speedup ≈0.879 and the per-shape 0.879/0.920/0.892 values for 1/8/64 tokens, remove or qualify the summary claim that every shape was lifted to 0.925/0.990/1.009, and reconcile best_geo_mean between .ledger.json (1.6234) and optimize_definition_output.json (1.5467) so downstream reporting cites one verified value. Do not cite the round-2 in-round speedups as achieved results.

findings.evidence: correctness.jsonl:1-3 (shapes [7,2,128], [83,4,512], [3,8,2048]) and timing.jsonl:1-5 (shapes [1,8,7168], [8,8,7168], [64,8,7168], [512,8,7168], [4096,8,7168]); .best_kernel.py:100-120 (block_m starts at 16 and is halved until it divides num_tokens, so T=7, 83 and 3 all select block_m=1; block_n=1024 only for H divisible by 1024, so H=7168 gives BN=1024). evaluate.json:19-131 reports abs_err/rel_err null for all five timing entries, and .ledger.json:225-226 reports max_abs_error 0.0 only for the three -correctness entries.
findings.reason: Every explicit correctness workload takes the block_m=1 branch (T=7, 83, 3), while all five benchmarked timing shapes with H=7168 and T=64/512/4096 take the new BM=16 mask-free path that is the entire round-2 optimization (.ledger.json:190-207). Consequently the optimized tiling branch — the one whose arithmetic and grid/offset math changed, including the flat m*(K*H)+n+k*H addressing with BM=16 and BN=1024 — has no supplied correctness case; static evidence cannot confirm that the timing phase performs numerical validation because its entries report null errors. This is a coverage limitation inherited from the extracted workload set (3 cases, bf16 only), not a candidate-code defect.
findings.requested_change: Add at least one correctness workload that selects block_m>1 with BN=1024, e.g. [64,8,7168] bf16 with routed_scaling_factor 2.5, so the BM=16 mask-free path and its flat-offset addressing are numerically validated; keep the existing 3 cases unchanged. Do not treat timing-phase PASSED status as numerical validation of the optimized branch.

findings.evidence: review.json:1-5 — {"policy": "gate", "status": "SKIPPED_EXPLICIT", "skip_review": true, "subject_sha256": "826c4f867f594787b9eb4877aa4e8f5b34e67ec4fb2dc4018bfd10c4847d62cb"}. Compare evaluation-contract.json:248 (bundle_id sha256:86f4c5cc9ca970a7533ea91e9bf45484fe103e9c40341c7409ac63309a13c987), :249 (benchmark_fingerprint sha256:f971d2f2b1519dec0031793fda97b692476776342143dbbd0a6aa28c058c5329) and optimize_definition_output.json:100 (solution_sha256 96b0e8e40b23afe9a654d9e1afdb120046c97edebeccea5d998c212fa8491196).
findings.reason: The only supplied test-contract review artifact is an explicit skip whose subject_sha256 matches neither the candidate under review (96b0e8e4…) nor the evaluation-contract bundle_id (86f4c5cc…) nor the benchmark fingerprint (f971d2f2…). It therefore provides no acceptance evidence for this candidate's test contract and must not be read as approval of the oracle/workloads used for this solution. I assessed that contract directly from the supplied catalog instead: oracle.py:4-5 computes input.float().sum(dim=1).mul(routed_scaling_factor).to(input.dtype) without importing or calling the candidate, oracle.py:17-24 uses bf16 atol=rtol=1.5e-2 matching the 0.015 tolerance in correctness.jsonl/timing.jsonl, oracle.py:28-36 compares the single declared output and returns a boolean-verdict mapping, and definition.json:19-25 declares one output with no mutation/alias — so I found no P0 contract defect, only the evidence-binding gap.
findings.requested_change: Re-run review_tests against the current subject sha256 96b0e8e4… (or record an explicit skip bound to that exact sha and to bundle_id sha256:86f4c5cc… / benchmark_fingerprint sha256:f971d2f2…), so the downstream gate has test-contract evidence that actually names this candidate. Do not carry forward the 826c4f86… skip as acceptance for this solution.
